qt: to the Commission Elena Yoncheva (ECR), Taner Kabilov (ECR) Subject:

Directive (EU) 2016/681 provides that passenger name record (PNR) data may be processed solely for the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of terrorist offences and serious crime. According to public statements by the Bulgarian Minister of Interior1, information concerning the international travel of identifiable persons enjoying immunity was disclosed. This raises concerns that data originating from Bulgaria’s Passenger Information Unit or the PNR system may have been accessed, used or disclosed outside the purposes and procedural safeguards established by Directive (EU) 2016/681 and EU data protection law, particularly in the light of the strict limitations imposed by the Court of Justice of the European Union on the use and retention of PNR data. 1.
Does the Commission consider the public disclosure of PNR-derived travel data concerning identifiable persons enjoying immunity to be compatible with EU data protection law?

Does the Commission consider that, if such information was disclosed without a legal basis, this would constitute a breach of the principles of purpose limitation, confidentiality and security of processing?

Will the Commission assess Bulgaria’s compliance with Directive (EU) 2016/681, including with regard to access logging, oversight of access to and use of PNR data, and safeguards against unlawful disclosure, and, where appropriate, take the necessary measures to ensure compliance with EU law?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.10.2026) Directive (EU) 2016/6811 (PNR Directive) regulates the processing of passenger name record (PNR) data pertaining to all passengers on any scheduled or non-scheduled flights, only for the purposes of fighting terrorism and serious crime. Such processing by national competent authorities must comply with a set of specific safeguards, as well as with the data protection principles of purpose limitation, necessity, proportionality, confidentiality, and security. This Directive, as interpreted by the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) in its Judgment in Case C817/19, requires that any disclosure of PNR data by a Passenger Information Unit be reviewed against these safeguards and principles. The Commission is not in a position to comment on the specific facts referred to by the Honourable Members, nor to verify, on the basis of public statements, whether the information concerned originated from PNR data or elsewhere, including whether it was lawfully disclosed. The assessment of individual instances of access to, disclosure of, or further processing of personal data falls within the competence of the relevant national authorities, including national supervisory authorities responsible for monitoring compliance with data protection rules. The Commission monitors the implementation by the Member States of the PNR Directive, as interpreted by the CJEU. An evaluation of the Directive is currently ongoing2, with a view to checking how the instrument is implemented at national level and assessing whether it remains fit-for-purpose to address current challenges as part of the EU’s overall security system. Where appropriate, the Commission may make use of the instruments at its disposal in order to ensure compliance with EU law.
1 Directive (EU) 2016/681 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the use of

passenger name record (PNR) data for the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of terrorist offences and serious crime; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2016/681/oj/eng. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/14437-Passenger-name-record-PNRdata-evaluation-of-Directive_en.
